messages.author: e1c430550f86b1f6
messages.subject: change point detection
parts:
Hi all,

I’m trying out to fit a time series that can have 0 or 1 change point using the sample model from Ch 11.2 of the manual.

To determine if the time series has a change-point or not, would I need to do comparison model (via loo) between 1-change model developed and a model with no change point?  Or, would s being close to 1 is sufficient?

Many thanks,

Andy

messages.author: 1d05bb6779340540
messages.subject: Re: change point detection
parts:
That's an excellent question. It often happens that the null model can be approximated by the alternative model when coefficients go toward zero, for example. However, if you compare models you should also take their complexity into account. If the null model fits just as well it should be preferred by your choice of model comparison, because it has less parameters.

J

messages.author: f53f4ca2c430170d
messages.subject: Re: change point detection
parts:
If the changepoint exists, do you know when it occurs?  It's going to be really hard to tell the difference between a one-change-point system with a small change-point effect from a zero-change-point system unless you know where the change-point is.  Even then you would need a lot of data around the change-point time.

I'm only bringing this up because it's not clear that your specific question matters.  I agree with Jan that a simpler model is often preferable for various reasons but in this case I don't think one parameter is going to make a big difference unless you have special requirements (e.g., someone has declared that there must be a hypothesis test).

Krzysztof

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
parts:
The change-point model is an expansion of the non-change-point model.
Without a prior on where the changepoint is or a prior on there being
a changepoint, a predictive comparison should favor the change-point model.

You could also fit a changepoint and compare the posterior of the
two components to see if they are much different and how they compare
to the non-changepoint model. That is, do some posterior predictive
comparisons.

- Bob

Bob - Thanks for the note.

The use case is for online change point detection over time. My assumption is that the underlying generation process would jump from one state to another (and the jump is “big" compared to observation error)

At time=t, I have new observation y[n] and old data y[1:n-1] and I want to know the probability of y[n] is generated from a state that is different from that had generated y[1..n-1].

Intuitively, I thought of fitting a change point model to y[1.. n] and check for existence of change point around n. Perhaps, there are better ways?

Thanks,

Andy

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
parts:
There are times when we fit unrelated models, or we have models coming from different sources, and predictive model comparison is one way to evaluate these. Especially the new form where we get the contribution of loo (or waic) for each data point.

But if you have a model (in this case, the change-point model in which the size of the change is an unknown parameter) which includes the smaller model (in this case, the no-change-point model, which is theta=0) as a special case, i’d rather just fit the big model. If you want to say, hey, let’s use the smaller model because it’s simpler and easier to work with, then, sure, I do think that loo or waic can be a way to make this decision. But I definitely wouldn’t frame it as “To determine if the time series has a change-point or not.” The time series, whatever it is, has a change point at every time. The question might be, “Is a change point necessary to model these data?” That’s a question I could get behind.

Does this help?
A

would rather an explicit prior on a continuous cut point and
then a discretization that puts the prior probability of

messages.author: fc5d3270037d7478
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
parts: In terms of coding, Andrew's proposed model should actually be easier in some sense, as it doesnt require marginalizing any discrete parameters. Change points at all time periods is equivalent to letting the relevant parameter vary over time, which for Stan usually just means declaring the parameter as a vector of length T and using a loop or a vectorized equivalent to estimate all T of the parameters (which can have a hierarchical prior if appropriate or independent priors).

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
parts:
I never understand specifically what's Andrew's suggesting.
I think the takeaway on model-non-comparison was this:

if you have a model (in this case, the change-point model in
which the size of the change is an unknown parameter) which
includes the smaller model (in this case, the no-change-point
model, which is theta=0) as a special case, i’d rather just fit
the big model.

My guess is that he has a whole suite of models of varying
granularity in mind. Because he goes on to say
The time series, whatever it is, has a change point at every time.

This implies to me that Andrew wants to unask the question of
whether the sequence has 0, 1, or T-1 change points? By definition
the sequence has T-1 observations. So it's just a question of what you want
to model.

But it's not a simple modeling change.

The no change-point model is easy

for (t in 1:T)
y[t] ~ normal(mu, sigma);

Pardon the non-vectorization --- it's just trying to make it unambiguous
there's a single mu and sigma and T different y.

Allowing one change point you need to marginalize out as
in the manual. Then it's a question of how you model where
the change occurs --- for a proper prior on a latent continuous
change point, you need the CDF differences (for same reason
as in our last discussion here on CDF diffs for rounding). Or you
can just hack it up as uniform as I did in the example in the manual
where the times are evenly spaced.

But when you allow T-1 change points, all of a sudden you're back
to something like the first model, with a time series

for (t in 1:T)
y[t] ~ normal(mu[t], sigma);

Assuming no stochastic volatility (i.e., a fixed sigma). Then you
need a prior for mu, probably one based on autoregression.

At least I think that's what's going on here.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
parts:
I think that makes is more obvious where the confusion is. I think there are those people who when asking the question "Where is the change point?" want a decision between

There is a change point at s and its size (difference between e, l) is such.
OR
There is not enough evidence for a change point anywhere

And then there are people who want an answer to

Suppose there is a change point, where could it be and what would its size be?

The answer to the last question could of course be: there is very little evidence for a very small change point here, which is unsatisfying for NHST-trained people, who want to know if it's signifiant or not.

J

On Wednesday, September 2, 2015 at 1:56:34 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
I never understand specifically what's Andrew's suggesting.
I think the takeaway on model-non-comparison was this:

  if you have a model (in this case, the change-point model in
  which the size of the change is an unknown parameter) which
  includes the smaller model (in this case, the no-change-point
  model, which is theta=0) as a special case, i’d rather just fit
  the big model.

My guess is that he has a whole suite of models of varying
granularity in mind.  Because he goes on to say

  The time series, whatever it is, has a change point at every time.

This implies to me that Andrew wants to unask the question of
whether the sequence has 0, 1, or T-1 change points?  By definition
the sequence has T-1 observations. So it's just a question of what you want
to model.

But it's not a simple modeling change.

The no change-point model is easy

   for (t in 1:T)
     y[t] ~ normal(mu, sigma);

Pardon the non-vectorization --- it's just trying to make it unambiguous
there's a single mu and sigma and T different y.

Allowing one change point you need to marginalize out as
in the manual.  Then it's a question of how you model where
the change occurs --- for a proper prior on a latent continuous
change point, you need the CDF differences (for same reason
as in our last discussion here on CDF diffs for rounding).  Or you
can just hack it up as uniform as I did in the example in the manual
where the times are evenly spaced.

But when you allow T-1 change points, all of a sudden you're back
to something like the first model, with a time series

  for (t in 1:T)
   y[t] ~ normal(mu[t], sigma);

Assuming no stochastic volatility (i.e., a fixed sigma).  Then you
need a prior for mu, probably one based on autoregression.

At least I think that's what's going on here.

- Bob


> On Sep 2, 2015, at 1:16 AM, Jonah <jga...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> In terms of coding, Andrew's proposed model should actually be easier in some sense, as it doesnt require marginalizing any discrete parameters. Change points at all time periods is equivalent to letting the relevant parameter vary over time, which for Stan usually just means declaring the parameter as a vector of length T and using a loop or a vectorized equivalent to estimate all T of the parameters (which can have a hierarchical prior if appropriate or independent priors).

messages.author: da33143a8db60ce8
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] change point detection
parts:
Hi, there are 2 issues here.

First is the distribution of change points over time. As Bob notes, I prefer to avoid change points entirely as I think that every moment has its own changes. Something that looks roughly like discrete change points can be constructed using continuous change points with a long tailed distribution of the amount of change.

The second issue is, if we do have a model with a discrete change point at just one time, to avoid the question, “Is there a change point?” by saying that there definitely _is_ a change point of unknown magnitude.

It was the second point that I was trying to make in my response to that earlier question. I think of this second model as a bit of a compromise. Yes, it assumes a particular change point. But it is still a continuous-parameter model, and I like that.

A
